schools.summary: Gregory the Great frames the whole section: while Job keeps silence, Elihu, a younger person, enters upon many right and sound topics, yet not rightly, nor with a sound intention.
Gill reads the friends' silence as weariness — they ceased, resting as men do on a sabbath, leaving the way clear for another disputant.

Henry catches the irony that a young man is raised to moderate the elders' heat, and doubts their plea that Job was 'righteous in his own eyes' — a cover to save their credit, for he was really righteous before God.

Keil and Delitzsch note the prose introduction is pointed in the poetical accentuation and read the silence as the friends' exhaustion; Ellicott traces Elihu's pedigree — Buz the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother (Gen. 22:21) — as a mark of a real personage.
Clarke reports the variant 'righteous in their eyes' (LXX, Syriac, Arabic, Chaldee, a Kennicott MS, Symmachus), the friends now convinced Job was a holy man.

debates.question: Does the clause read 'righteous in his own eyes' or 'righteous in their eyes'?

sides.position: the received text — Job was righteous 'in his own eyes'
'in their eyes' (LXX, Syriac, Arabic, Chaldee, a Kennicott MS, Symmachus) — the friends now saw Job as holy

schools.summary: Gill dismisses the traditions that Elihu was Balaam the soothsayer or the Messiah — though the names might be strained toward Christ — taking him for a holy and good man.

Clarke reads the kindled wrath as zeal for God's justice, traces Buz and Ram/Aram, and takes 'justified himself' as Job 'justifying his soul' (naphsho); Wesley marks the pedigree for Elihu's honour and to evidence the history, and unfolds the name 'my God is he.'

Keil and Delitzsch render the wrath against Job (justified himself at God's expense) and the friends (found no answer, yet condemned); Ellicott points to Job 19:6, balancing it with Job's confession that God was his salvation (Job 13:16).
Gill: Elihu took part with neither but blamed both; the friends' double failure was to find no answer and yet condemn Job all the same.
Clarke: they condemned Job yet could not answer his reasonings; Wesley: no answer to the main cause, and yet they condemned him as a bad man.
Ellicott states the injustice bare — they could not reply nor deny Job's account, yet concluded he must be wicked because God had smitten him, reasoning backward from affliction to guilt.
Henry's impartial moderator is displeased with both, for seldom is a quarrel carried so far without fault on both sides; the seeker of truth must separate the precious from the vile.
Gill: Elihu waited until Job had made an end and the three friends had said all they had to say.

Keil and Delitzsch read 'had waited for Job with words,' the perfect for the pluperfect, deferring because the three were older in days; Ellicott lays out Elihu's intermediate line — admitting Job's integrity, holding the afflictions to have a disciplinary object, with lofty ideas of God's righteousness, leading Job toward the whirlwind answer.
Henry commends the modesty of deferring to seniority, the rules of precedency that keep order, which the young pay and will one day receive.
Gill: there was no answer that could be called an answer; the aged, reputed wise and knowing, were quite nonplussed and silenced.
Keil and Delitzsch note the peculiar vocabulary of the Elihu section, the rare verb (cognate with the Arabic for drawing back in fear) picturing a man who 'stood back and was afraid.'
Henry reads Elihu's diffidence as not cowardice — like Moses his face shone and he knew it not — urging that we be swift to hear and slow to speak, especially against venerated elders.

themes: the rare verb of drawing back

schools.summary: Gill: since no answer was left in the elders, Elihu undertakes one himself, but first apologizes for his youth.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'I am young in days, and ye are hoary... I stood back and was afraid'; Ellicott finds the manner of his coming forward full of character, a picture of the times and habits.
Clarke: among the Asiatics the young never spoke before their elders, above all in controversy; Wesley: the fear of being thought forward and presumptuous.
Henry makes the verse a model for the young — abilities without assurance, suspicious of one's own judgment against venerated elders, yet knowing when to speak as well as when to keep silence.

themes: I am young and ye are very old

schools.summary: Gill: 'days should speak' means men of many days, whose place and duty it is to speak and instruct their juniors, and from whom profit may justly be looked for.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'Let age speak, and the multitude of years teach wisdom,' the opinion Elihu held until a deeper consideration overturned it.
Clarke: men were reputed wise in proportion to their years, the boasted wisdom of the East lying largely in treasured proverbs and maxims.
Henry weighs the maxim's truth and limits — age gives advantage in judging, a reason for the old to learn and teach and the young to attend; it is a good lodging with an old disciple.

themes: the concession about to be corrected

schools.summary: Gill takes it as a correction of Elihu's former sentiment — a spirit in men of every age — and allows the common reading of the rational soul in every man, by which he knows and reasons.

Clarke reads an afflatus in mankind, the breath of the Almighty giving understanding (Gen. 2:7), the light that lighteth every man (John 1:9) bearing witness with our spirit (Rom. 8:16); Wesley: the Spirit of God, giving to whom he pleases.

Ellicott renders 'it is the spirit in man, and the breath of the Almighty,' the Mosaic language, so that not years but the spirit and illumination of the Almighty make a man pre-eminent; Keil and Delitzsch ground man's very life in the Spirit of God.

debates.question: Is the 'spirit in man' the human rational soul or the inbreathed Spirit of God?

sides.position: the rational soul native to every man (Gill's first sense)
the inbreathed Spirit and breath of the Almighty, who gives understanding where he will

themes: there is a spirit in man
the rational soul or the Spirit of God
understanding a gift not of years

schools.summary: Gill ranges the senses of 'great' — in rank, in number, in years, as teachers — men wise in worldly things yet not in the reasons of God's providence.
Clarke: the aged had wise sayings collected but no discretion in applying them; Wesley glosses 'judgment' as what is just and right, the very thing they failed to discern.
Ellicott takes 'great men' as old men, or the many (cf. Job 12:2, 'wisdom shall die with you'); Keil and Delitzsch read the couplet as of a piece with the argument.
Henry: it is folly to subscribe with implicit faith to any; even the aged may err and should welcome instruction from their juniors, a poor and wise child being better than an old and foolish king.

themes: great men are not always wise

schools.summary: Gill notes the singular address to Job and each friend — though young, if Elihu has the Spirit of God and the inspiration of the Almighty, he may say something worth hearing.
Ellicott reads 'I said' as equivalent to 'I say,' the present resolve ripened out of former convictions.

Henry gathers the force of the 'therefore' — reason is every man's honour and none may engross it; we must hear reason even from inferiors, as a clear eye sees further on level ground than a purblind eye from a mountain.

themes: reason the endowment of every man
a hearing claimed not by years

schools.summary: Gill hears real eagerness — Elihu waited for their words as for the rain, until they had wholly done.
Clarke notes the variant 'your arguments' (Kennicott, De Rossi) and the fine irony of 'whilst ye searched out words,' the elders casting about for something to say.
Henry makes the patient hearing itself an argument — Elihu attended though the elders were slow and unready; those who have heard may speak, by the mutual liberty of debate.

themes: the irony of searching out words

schools.summary: Gill: Elihu attended closely, got within them, the better to be sure of the failure he now reports.
Clarke notes a reading 'your testimonies,' and insists that though they spoke multitudes of words none confuted Job; Wesley glosses 'convinced' as convinced by solid and satisfactory answers.
Ellicott judges no one had touched the main point; Keil and Delitzsch render 'no one who refuted Job... from you,' the asyndeton marking a feeling that outruns the connectives of calm speech.
Henry: having heard them out, Elihu knew what to say; he that answers before hearing, or by halves, is impertinent and imperious.
Gill reads it as a caution against their being wise in their own conceits — all true wisdom is of God, not found out by men.

Clarke: the friends boast of having found the true system, and take 'God thrusts him down, not man' as proof Job is wicked; Wesley: God left them to their weakness lest they ascribe the silencing of Job to their own wisdom, an argument that does not satisfy Elihu.
Ellicott: Elihu resolved to speak lest they think themselves wise and suppose God was afflicting Job on account of his sins.
Henry: it is time to speak when error is dressed as piety and God's judgments are vouched for men's pride — or lest they think the wisest course to leave Job to God.

themes: lest ye say we have found wisdom
God thrusteth him down not man

schools.summary: Gill: Job had not directed his words against Elihu, who comes to the debate calm and unprovoked, with truth, God's glory, and Job's good in view.
Clarke: no party to the quarrel and no cause of irritation — he speaks for truth, not conquest, and will not answer with the friends' inflamed speeches.

Henry unfolds the double resolve — Elihu allows Job's protestations of integrity (only a gentle reproof for his passionate words) and will not repeat the friends' matter or manner; why do over again (actum agere) what is done?

themes: he hath not directed his words against me
neither will I answer with your speeches

schools.summary: Gill reads the elders as men thunderstruck, astonished that a young man should speak and that they, for all their years, were left with nothing to say.
Clarke records Good's rendering that their speeches are dissipated, but prefers to take it of Job's friends, weary of their repetitions and giving up the contest.
Ellicott gives the force with the present tense — 'they are amazed... they have not a word to say' — a silence that is a defeat, not a pause.
Henry finds the stage cleared — the friends stood still and yielded the floor — and the pleasant conjecture that Elihu is the book's penman writing as historian of the scene.
Gill: Elihu waited to see whether they would reply or object, and finding none, went on.
Clarke: 'I waited to hear if they had anything to reply to Job; and when I found them speechless, then I ventured to come forward.'

Ellicott notes some read the clause as a question, 'shall I wait because they speak not?'; Keil and Delitzsch open the long declaration, dwelling on the peculiar defective spellings that mark the Elihu speeches as a distinct layer.
Henry hears the pressure beneath — Elihu uneasy, in pain to be delivered, while musing the fire burned, shut up in his bones as the prophet Jeremiah felt it.

themes: the defective forms of the Elihu speeches
the fire shut up in his bones

schools.summary: Gill: Elihu takes his turn to answer Job, since what the friends offered was insufficient and unsuitable to the case.
Clarke fixes the Hebrew 'I will recite my portion' (aaneh chelki), reading Job as a drama recited for public instruction, Elihu a bystander taking a part he cannot close, which God must decide.
Henry hears the modesty tempering the boldness — no definitive sentence, for the judgment is the Lord's; Elihu submits his portion like the rest, with no arrogance, only asking a fair hearing.

themes: I will answer also my part

schools.summary: Gill: full of matter, not empty words but solid reasoning — like an able minister full of the word, a treasure in an earthen vessel, the opposite of the fool's abundance.
Clarke reads 'matter' as millim, wise sayings, and hears in the second clause St. Paul's 'the love of Christ constraineth us,' Elihu under the Spirit's influence and concerned for all.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the spirit of my inner nature constraineth me,' the defective spelling marking the section, the pressure of a conviction that will not be held in.
Henry: a man with much to say; when the aged are drawn dry God fills even the young for the church's edifying, the fulness a stewardship not to be buried.
Gill, with Ben Gersom, reads the belly as a bottle of wine stopped close, the new wine apt to ferment and needing vent.
Clarke fills in the whole picture of goat-skin wine-bags, new wine in effervescence bursting an unvented or old skin (Matt. 9:17), such skins serving for wine, water, butter, and dry goods.
Ellicott glosses 'new bottles' as wine-skins (Matt. 9:17); Keil and Delitzsch render 'my interior... like new bottles it is ready to burst.'
Henry: never did nurse whose breasts were gorged long to be drawn as Elihu longed to speak — a need, not a mere wish.

themes: the ferment that must find vent

schools.summary: Gill: Elihu resolves to speak and be eased; the minister's parallel — the Gospel a word in season, refreshing both others and himself.
Clarke keeps the wine-skin figure running — the bottle must be opened to be saved: 'I will open my mouth.'
Henry reads the refreshment as more than relief — the pleasure of doing good and speaking for God's glory, against the grief of a minister silenced and thrust into a corner.

themes: I will speak that I may be refreshed
the joy of speaking for God

schools.summary: Gill: Elihu renounces both temptations — Job's poverty and the friends' grandeur — for neither poor nor rich is to be regarded in a cause, but only its right.
Clarke reads a pledge to speak truth without fear or favour; 'flattering titles' is putting a false name on a man — titles of real office proper, but the bombastic titles of the East not.
Henry: flatter neither Job in his affliction nor the friends in their prosperity, for the law forbids countenancing poor or rich to pervert justice (Exod. 23:3).
Gill: Elihu was never brought up to flattering language, nor used to it, nor could give such titles in conscience.

Clarke: were he to flatter, God might justly consume him — his Maker made him for truth; he gathers Eastern examples of swelling titles clothing kings in the attributes of Deity. Wesley: to eye God's majesty as our Maker is the surest cure of flattery.

Ellicott weighs the estimate of Elihu — an empty arrogant talker to some, a wise pious friend to others — and inclines to the kinder view since God passes no condemnation on him; the closing verses a soliloquy.
Henry: the more closely we eye God's majesty and dread his justice, the less we fear or flatter men, for God will put lying and flattering lips to silence.

debates.question: How is Elihu to be estimated — a wise and pious friend or a presumptuous, empty talker?

sides.position: a wise and pious friend who came nearest the truth of Job's case, and whom God does not condemn
an empty and arrogant talker — right in his topics, yet not right in intention

outliers.note: Frames the whole section by judging that Elihu enters upon many right and sound topics, yet not rightly nor with a sound intention — a mixed verdict the later witnesses debate.

themes: I know not to give flattering titles
my Maker would take me away
the fear of God that forbids flattery
